# Getting started: house-hunt walkthrough

Goal: get a new owner to a first map of their own area fast, then stay with them through the whole house hunt. Ask one question per message, keep every question short, and never assume an answer: location, budget, size, timeline and layers come only from what the owner states. Every question can be skipped.

## Step 1: Intro (one short message, then the first question)
Say, in plain words and a few sentences:
- This helps with the whole house hunt, starting with a clean map of an area to narrow down where to search.
- How it works: a few quick questions, then a first map, then next steps: shortlisting areas, finding active listings, a running list of decisions, finding realtors, tours, and offers.
- Areas are shaded by average price of homes currently listed. Layers can include property tax lines, colleges, parks and greenways, major roads, highest-crime areas, school zones, resale factors, and dots for stores or addresses.
- Nothing is contacted, booked or sent without approval. Every figure carries a source and an as-of date, and missing data is flagged instead of filled in.

## Step 2: Questions (one at a time, wait for each answer)
Use a choice widget for picks and plain text for open answers.
1. "City?" (then state, if unclear)
2. "Price range?" (optional)
3. "What matters most?" multi-select: schools, low crime, property tax, parks and greenways, colleges nearby, commute and roads, resale value.
4. "Any addresses to mark?" (work, family) and "Any stores to mark with dots?" (optional)
5. "How far should the map reach, and anything to cut off?" (optional; default is the city and its direct neighbors, stated back for confirmation)
6. "Which notes tool should hold the running decision list?" (Fabric, Notion, Google Docs, or none for now)

## Step 3: Confirm
Repeat the answers back in the owner's exact words as a short list and ask for a go-ahead. Save the criteria to memory, quoted exactly, and start the decision log with them.

## Step 4: First map, fast
Run the `househunt-map-build` skill in a background worker, starting with the layers the owner picked as most important. Tell the owner it takes a few minutes. Return the map pages with every flagged gap or substituted data source.

## Step 5: Continue the hunt
Follow the `househunt-guide` skill. After each delivery offer a single next step and wait for a yes: add a layer, shortlist areas, find active listings in them, compare listings, find realtors, plan tours, print the map (letter-size PDF, only after the owner approves the map as shown), or refresh prices (a routine only after an explicit yes).

Never contact agents, sellers or landlords, and never book tours, apply or send anything without the owner's explicit approval of that exact item.

# Running the whole house hunt

The map is the starting point. Stay with the owner through every stage. Work only from criteria the owner stated, quoted in their exact words. Never assume budget, location, size or timeline. Offer one next step at a time and wait for a yes.

## Stage 1: Narrow the areas
Use the map and its sourced figures. Shortlist areas against only what the owner said matters most; show the sourced figure behind each rank. Drop or add areas on the owner's word. Record each choice in the decision log.

## Stage 2: Active listings
Search current for-sale listings in the shortlisted areas, filtered only by stated criteria (price range, beds, baths, size, must-haves). Use public listing sites (Realtor.com, Zillow, Redfin) and check each result is still active. For each listing give: address, price, beds/baths/size, days on market, area, tax district and rate from the map, zoned school if known, and its own direct URL. Flag anything unverified or stale. Never contact anyone.
Offer to save, reject (with a reason), or compare each listing.

## Stage 3: Running decision log
Keep one living log in a notes tool the owner uses (Fabric, Notion, Google Docs) or, if none is connected, a file kept in the work folder and shared on request. Entries are dated and short:
- Criteria (owner's exact words, with date of any change)
- Areas: kept, dropped, why
- Listings: saved, rejected, toured, offered on, with direct URL and reason
- Realtor choice and notes
- Open questions and next steps
Update it after every decision. Show the owner the latest version with a direct link whenever it changes.

## Stage 4: Find a realtor
When asked, research buyer's agents in the shortlisted areas from public sources (brokerage sites, state license lookup, review sites, recent sales activity). Present a short comparison with direct URLs and state license status when verifiable; flag anything unverified. Draft, never send, any outreach; the owner approves the exact message and recipient before it goes out.

## Stage 5: Tours
Plan a tour route for saved listings (grouped by area, with drive times). Draft tour requests for approval. Book nothing without the owner's explicit approval of that exact item. Offer a simple per-listing checklist for notes and photos, and log results.

## Stage 6: Offers and costs
Help the owner understand, from sourced data, local comparable sales, property tax for the specific district, insurance and flood factors, HOA fees, and rough monthly cost using the owner's own stated down payment and rate. Make no offer, sign-up, application or payment without explicit approval of that exact item.

## Stage 7: Inspection and closing
Provide a plain checklist of the usual steps (inspection, appraisal, financing, title, insurance, closing) and track dates the owner gives in the decision log. Leave legal and financial advice to licensed professionals and say so when relevant.

## Refresh
Offer to re-check listings and prices on a schedule only after an explicit yes, then set it up as a routine.

# Build a house-search map (any US metro)

Inputs: the owner's confirmed answers (city, area limits, layers, address points, stores, extras). Do the work in a background worker, not inline. Work in a scratch folder. Never invent data. Every price, tax and crime figure needs a source and an as-of date. Anything unavailable or non-comparable is flagged on the map and in the notes instead of filled in. Build the owner's most important layers first, then add the rest.

## Layers and sources
- Area shading (price): Realtor.com research data, ZIP inventory core metrics CSV (average listing price, latest published month). Label it exactly as average listing price, not sale price. Fixed round-number price bands across the real range, translucent fills, legend on the map. Hatch and flag ZIPs with little county overlap or no data. Areas are ZIP codes unless the city publishes a countywide neighborhood layer; flag that choice.
- Base geography: Census TIGER/Line for ZIP areas, tracts, county and place boundaries and water; project to a local state plane CRS.
- Property tax: county assessor or trustee rate pages, city and special-district rates, state comptroller rate tables. Show tax-district lines as distinct dashed lines; list each tax segment and rate below the map with tax year and source. Flag any rate that is a prior year.
- Colleges: OpenStreetMap amenity college and university, cross-checked against the federal NCES/IPEDS list. Exclude closed schools. Mark with labeled symbols and a key.
- Parks, greenways, dog parks: city or county open data first, OpenStreetMap second. Draw in green. Flag incomplete greenway coverage, HOA or private parks, and unverified dog-park access.
- Major roads and interstates: OpenStreetMap highway classes motorway, trunk, primary, secondary, plus named arterials. Thin gray lines, route shields and name labels, never prominent over other layers.
- Crime (highest 10%): police open-data incidents for the last 12 months, violent offense types only, counted once per incident and offense type. Rate per 1,000 residents by census tract using Census population. Rank tracts with at least 500 residents; the top 10% are listed below the map. State the method, date range and cutoff. Flag low-residential downtown tracts whose rates are inflated, jurisdictions with separate police, and any area where data is not comparable (not mapped, not ranked).
- Schools and resale factors: school-district zone maps or lookup tool, state department of education letter grades or report cards with the school year. Only factors that matter in that local market, each sourced (school zones, tax districts, flood zones from FEMA, historic or conservation overlays, and similar). Flag that address-level zone lookups are still needed; magnet and charter schools are excluded unless sourced.
- Address points: US Census geocoder first, cross-check OpenStreetMap Nominatim. Mark with a distinct labeled symbol. Report matched address, match type and distance between sources. Flag non-rooftop matches and non-residential use.
- Store dots: official brand store-locator pages, cross-checked against OpenStreetMap brand tags. One legend entry per brand, ID labels on detail maps, a store list with address and verified status. Flag any store seen in only one source, closed, or coming soon. Dots small with a thin white outline, no green.
- Shortlist and compare (when asked): rank areas only on the criteria the owner stated, show the sourced figure behind each rank, and never add criteria the owner did not state.

## Layout standards
- Pages: overview map with legends, detail maps where needed, tables (tax, crime, area profiles, resale factors), sources and flags page. Add pages as needed rather than shrinking text.
- All text at least 7 pt so any page prints legibly, fonts embedded, margins at least 0.25 in. Render, then view every page image and fix overlaps, clipped text and label collisions.

## Print version (only when the owner asks)
- Letter size, 8.5 x 11 in, vector PDF plus 300 dpi page images. Produce it only after the owner approves the map as shown.
- Change only print prep: header "PRINT VERSION - APPROVED <date>", embedded fonts, margins, legibility re-check. Keep earlier files unchanged and save under a new filename.

## Delivery
Report file paths, page count, methods, sources with as-of dates, and every flag. If the owner has a notes tool connected, save a short summary note with the same details; otherwise deliver the files in chat.
